title: Tank officer Keith Douglas turned the desert war into poems, then fell in Normandy
body: Keith Douglas, born in 1920, was a British poet and a tank officer with the Sherwood Rangers Yeomanry. When the Battle of El Alamein began in Egypt in October 1942 he was stuck in a staff job, so he drove to his regiment against orders, and fought across Libya until a mine wounded him at Wadi Zem Zem in January 1943. His prose memoir of those months, *Alamein to Zem Zem*, illustrated with his own drawings, came out in 1946; the [Commonwealth War Graves Commission](https://admin.cwgc.org/our-work/blog/remembering-the-poets-of-world-war-two/) calls it one of the most expressive accounts of the North Africa campaign. He recovered, fought again in Tunisia in 1943 and wrote poems there: “Aristocrats” is dated Tunisia 1943. In “Vergissmeinnicht”, a poem drawn from what he saw, soldiers come back to a battlefield three weeks on and find the German gunner who had hit the narrator’s tank, with a photograph signed by his girlfriend, Steffi. Its line “For here the lover and killer are mingled” sees both men in one. Douglas was killed in Normandy on 9 June 1944, three days after D-Day, aged 24.

slides.alt: Animation on a cream notebook page in pencil and ink: a route along a schematic coast of North Africa from El Alamein to Wadi Zem Zem and on to Tunisia, a drawn book, a photograph left in the sand, blue forget-me-nots, a line of the poem, then Normandy.

slides.takeaway: The memoir runs from El Alamein in Egypt to Wadi Zem Zem in Libya: it stops before Tunisia, where Douglas wrote his 1943 poems. He died in Normandy in 1944.

slides.heading: Memoir and poem
slides.text: Alamein to Zem Zem is a prose memoir of real events, from El Alamein in October 1942 to Wadi Zem Zem in January 1943. “Vergissmeinnicht” is a poem, drawn from what Douglas saw: a dead German gunner and his girlfriend’s photograph.

slides.question: In Keith Douglas’s poem “Vergissmeinnicht”, what do the soldiers find beside the dead German gunner?
slides.explanation: A photograph of his girlfriend, signed “Steffi. Vergissmeinnicht”, German for forget me not. They find it three weeks after the fight.
